title: In Defense of Jenny Jones
gist: A photographer's defense of 1990s tabloid TV argues that Jenny Jones — unlike Geraldo, Sally Jessy Raphael or the therapeutic Oprah/Dr. Phil format that replaced her — offered consequence-free frivolity rather than titillation disguised as journalism, and that the real 1990s corrosion was Seinfeld's abolition of moral learning. It traces the tabloid spirit of mockery from Plautus through The Apprentice to Trump, arguing that progressive euphemism substituted language for redistribution and produced the backlash.

themes.theme: The Jenny Jones murder and the limits of media liability

insights.claim: In March 1995 Jonathan Schmitz bought a 12-gauge shotgun and killed Scott Amedure three days after both men appeared on a Jenny Jones segment titled “Revealing Same-Sex Secret Crush,” and Schmitz was convicted of second-degree murder.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: The canonical case study for how a conflict-provocation content format converts into legal and reputational tail risk.
insights.locator: In March 1995, in Lake Orion, Michigan

insights.claim: A jury awarded Scott Amedure’s parents $29.3 million against the Jenny Jones show, but the Michigan Court of Appeals held the producers had no duty to foresee that a mentally ill guest would kill, and the host herself was never named as a defendant.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Foreseeability, not offensiveness, bounds producer liability for provoked-conflict formats — headline verdicts against media companies often do not survive appeal.
insights.locator: At trial, which the press dubbed

insights.claim: A televised-murder scandal dented ratings only briefly and the Jenny Jones show ran for eight more years, showing that a working television format is far more durable than the outrage attached to it.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Advertiser-boycott and scandal risk to entertainment franchises is usually transient; the format dies of formula fatigue, not of controversy.
insights.quote: Ratings dipped, but the show ran for eight more years.

themes.theme: Non-judgment as the competitive edge in 1990s tabloid TV

insights.claim: Geraldo Rivera and Sally Jessy Raphael sold interrogation and psychological diagnosis of their guests, which the author reads as titillation dressed up as journalism, while Jenny Jones treated the same guests as entertainment rather than social pathology.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Within one content genre, host posture is the real product differentiator — the same raw material reads as exploitation or as carnival depending on framing.
insights.quote: sold titillation disguised as journalism, a very shady business
insights.locator: Unless you thought about it

insights.claim: The defining trick of the Jenny Jones persona was occupying two positions at once — standing above the spectacle while participating in it — and dispensing the fifteen minutes of fame her guests wanted.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: A reusable model for any attention platform: hosts who are simultaneously inside and above the crowd retain audience trust that pure moralists and pure hucksters both lose.
insights.quote: Her gift was to be both above the fray and in it—an angel granting the fifteen minutes of fame her seemingly unhappy guests craved.
insights.locator: Jenny, on the other hand, was light on interrogation

insights.claim: Critics treated the host’s easy familiarity with her guests as a lack of seriousness, but the author argues it was the show’s one moral advantage, because the guests were never framed as damaged goods or as specimens.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Elite critical consensus about downmarket media reliably inverts the actual dignity ranking of the products it judges.
insights.quote: Jenny never condescended to her guests, or treated them as damaged goods, or, even worse, intriguing specimens
insights.locator: Unlike Geraldo Rivera and Sally Jessy Raphael

insights.claim: Jenny Jones was born Janina Stronski, had no high school degree and no broadcasting or journalism training, and reached daytime television via shoplifting, a strip-club hostess job, drumming behind Wayne Newton, and standup comedy.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: The most commercially effective mass-market hosts are manufactured by show business from below, not credentialed from above — a durable casting signal for talent-driven media.
insights.quote: Show business was my way out.
insights.locator: Born Janina Stronski

insights.claim: The show was originally formatted for women around hair, makeup, cooking and boyfriends before pivoting to dysfunctional-couple segments, a format drift toward conflict that raised its ceiling.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Format migration toward interpersonal conflict is the recurring monetization path of daytime and, later, social media attention.
insights.locator: The original format of Jenny Jones

themes.theme: Self-esteem as an American civil religion

insights.claim: A studio audience that had just booed a man for refusing to clean or brush his teeth cheered him seconds later when he appeared punching the air, because unapologetic self-belief had displaced the behavior being judged as the thing that mattered.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Audience approval attaches to displayed confidence rather than to conduct — the mechanism that later made shamelessness a winning strategy in politics and online media.
insights.locator: This was close to insanity

insights.claim: Decades of television psychology promoting self-esteem as the supreme virtue, and of participation trophies for children who played badly, turned positive reinforcement into a national identity project.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Frames the demand side for a half-century of self-help, wellness and personal-brand products as a civic ideology rather than a fad.
insights.quote: Positive reinforcement had become an American passion—a patriotism of the self.
insights.locator: For years, TV psychologists like Dr. Joyce Brothers

insights.claim: Guests defused hostile, holier-than-thou audience questions by invoking a single rule — never let other people’s expectations define you — which made shaming rhetorically inert.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Explains why public shaming campaigns fail against targets who have pre-committed to self-authorization; the tactic only works on people who accept the audience’s standing to judge.
insights.quote: Never let the expectations of others define you.
insights.locator: After her guests were (sort of) interviewed

themes.theme: Television as a solvent of moral judgment

insights.claim: Television works by immediacy rather than argument, dissolving judgment and manufacturing an undiscriminating tolerance for whatever it shows — which the author treats as the medium’s actual message.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: The structural case that visual-immediacy media erode normative filtering, now recapitulated at far higher velocity by short-form video feeds.
insights.quote: Television is a mesmeric medium that dissolves judgment in a crucible of visual immediacy. It creates a free-floating tolerance for everything.
insights.locator: Anyway, who cared?

insights.claim: A boy taught in school that killing is a crime and in church that it is a sin still never questioned the right of television cowboys and detectives to kill weekly, showing screen framing overriding formal moral instruction.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Institutional moral instruction loses to entertainment framing when the two conflict — relevant to any thesis about content regulation changing behavior.
insights.locator: Even though, as a boy, I’d learned in school

insights.claim: Projecting toddler photographs of the guests instantly silenced a jeering studio audience, the host’s reliable de-escalation device.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: A concrete, transferable technique for defusing a hostile crowd: replace the present subject with an image of their innocence.
insights.quote: Photographs are not static—they drift between past and present. They comfort us when they preserve continuity, but they unnerve us when they reveal the havoc of history.
insights.locator: One of Jenny’s gifts was her ability to pacify

insights.claim: The makeover segment encodes a specifically televisual proposition: that despair, dysfunction and social resentment are a surface style that can be restyled rather than conditions with causes.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: The founding premise of the makeover, wellness and personal-transformation economy — sell appearance change as a solution to structural distress.
insights.quote: despair, dysfunction, and social resentment might just be a “look” gone rogue
insights.locator: What mattered was that her makeover offered a television truth

themes.theme: Class taste, the 1995 moral panic, and elite misreading

insights.claim: In October 1995 Senator Joe Lieberman and William Bennett held a bipartisan press conference against daytime tabloid talk shows and pressed sponsors such as Kraft and Procter & Gamble to stop advertising on what they called cultural rot.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: The template for every subsequent advertiser-pressure campaign against a platform: political theater aimed at the CPG ad budget rather than at the content owner.
insights.locator: In October 1995, a few months after

insights.claim: The reformers’ appeal to “decent, average Americans” was incoherent because the average American was precisely the audience for tabloid TV, an early instance of elites legislating against the tastes of the majority they claim to speak for.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Watch for the same category error in content-moderation and culture-war campaigns — the audience being protected is the audience being described as deviant.
insights.locator: But in the 1990s, the concept of

insights.claim: Tabloid talk shows were built for a large Midwestern working-class audience that preferred the drama of open confrontation to Letterman’s cool detachment or Seinfeld’s ironic nihilism, making the 1990s taste split a class split rather than a moral one.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: The audience segmentation that later becomes the college/non-college political divide is visible in 1990s programming preferences a generation early.
insights.locator: Bennett and Lieberman styled themselves defenders

themes.theme: Seinfeld as the real corrosive, not tabloid TV

insights.claim: The genuine cultural threat of the 1990s was not Maury Povich or Jenny Jones but Seinfeld, whose nineteen-million-viewer sitcom removed learning, maturation and moral resolution from the form entirely.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: A reminder that the highest-status, most-praised mass product often carries the norm-shift that the moral panic aimed at the low-status product completely missed.
insights.quote: America didn’t need saving from Maury Povich or Jenny Jones. It needed saving from Seinfeld.
insights.locator: But in the 1990s, the concept of

insights.claim: Earlier sitcoms preserved a residue of self-reflection — Hawkeye savaged bureaucracy but saved lives, Archie Bunker’s bigotry was tempered by empathy — while Seinfeld made love a neurosis, friendship disposable and altruism nonexistent.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Traces the exact point where mainstream comedy stopped underwriting moral development, a precondition for later ironic and nihilistic online culture.
insights.quote: the most villainous sitcom ever made
insights.locator: Seinfeld was revolutionary

themes.theme: The ridicule cycle: mockery, therapy, reality TV

insights.claim: By the early 2000s reality television displaced tabloid talk shows by offering unscripted confrontation plus the voyeuristic spectacle of an unraveling, now with prize money attached.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Format succession in cheap unscripted content follows escalating stakes; the incumbent format is displaced by one that adds real consequences.
insights.locator: But by the early 2000s

insights.claim: After 9/11 America became less willing to ridicule openly, and Oprah and Dr. Phil converted the tabloid show into therapeutic theater in which guests were reframed from caricatures into survivors of misfortune.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Marks the birth of the wellness-and-self-help content economy as a rebranding of the same voyeurism, with sincerity as the sales mechanism.
insights.quote: their lavish sincerity was engineered to sell products
insights.locator: But something else was happening

insights.claim: The impulse to ridicule an Other in order to shore up the status quo is permanent and only changes costume — from Plautus’s scolding women and effeminate foreigners to Jenny’s rebellious teens and cross-dressers to therapeutic television’s disguised shaming.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Treat public shaming as a constant with rotating targets rather than a phenomenon that any reform can retire; useful for forecasting the next respectable form of mockery.
insights.quote: The need to ridicule may change its shape over time, but it never disappears. Call it the tabloid spirit.
insights.locator: The need to ridicule may change its shape

insights.claim: The Apprentice staged hyper-capitalism as a morality play in which self-promotion and ruthless strategizing were the rewarded virtues, with a televised ritual of humiliation as its only iconic moment.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: The show that trained a mass audience to read business as a jungle contest is the same asset that built the political brand — entertainment IP as political infrastructure.
insights.quote: It was pure jungle beneath the business casual.
insights.locator: To answer that question, one need only watch

themes.theme: Euphemism, backlash, and Trump as heir to the tabloid spirit

insights.claim: The substitution of the euphemisms of social equality for social equality itself was, as David Foster Wallace argued, a gift to conservatives, because it kept progressives arguing over descriptions while factories closed in Pennsylvania and reopened in China.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: A causal account of why language politics displaced redistribution politics — the substitution left the trade and manufacturing story to the other side.
insights.quote: Orwellian substitution of the euphemisms of social equality for social equality itself
insights.locator: Tabloid TV, which made a living ridiculing

insights.claim: The word “wokeness” insulted the very people it was meant to awaken, and non-college voters rejected being told their ordinary speech was offensive and their lives defined by privilege.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: The naming of a reform movement is itself a political variable; a label that implies the audience is asleep guarantees the backlash it produces.
insights.quote: Wokeness, impervious to nuance, claimed the high ground, but its very name insulted those it intended to wake.
insights.locator: It’s easy to dismiss tabloid TV as lowbrow

insights.claim: The author’s stated price of that moralizing was two Donald Trump presidencies, a backlash that in his reading erased thirty years of progressive corrections.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Frames the political cycle as a reaction function to elite moral policing rather than to economics alone — a lens for handicapping how durable the reversal is.
insights.quote: a backlash that flattened any and all progressive “corrections” of the past thirty years
insights.locator: The price of course was the two presidencies

insights.claim: Trump is best understood as the heir of tabloid television, functioning simultaneously as the defiant narcissistic guest and as the outraged heckling audience.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: A predictive model of the style: expect escalation of mockery and humiliation rituals rather than platform argument, because that is the inherited format.
insights.quote: Successful demagogues know instinctively that in order to “read” the room, you must become the room.
insights.locator: Certainly, it’s beyond the scope of this essay

insights.claim: In the 2015 Republican debates derision and name-calling swept aside nine rivals who spoke in canned platitudes, an early demonstration that tabloid affect beats message discipline in a crowded field.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: In fragmented, many-candidate fields, attention-dominant style outperforms consensus messaging — applies to primaries and to attention markets generally.
insights.quote: “You’re fired!” was just an early version of “Drain the swamp!”
insights.locator: The price of course was the two presidencies

insights.claim: Anti-Trump elites now compete to find the ugliest names for the man they detest, adopting the very jeering register whose bad manners they once looked down on in tabloid TV.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: The derisive register is not confined to one political side; the norm that collapsed was class-coded refinement, not partisan civility.
insights.quote: In Trump’s USA, they strain to find the ugliest names—and some are truly ugly—to describe the man they detest. So much for middle-class refinement.
insights.locator: And what a surprising world we live in!

insights.claim: The author defends frivolity and vulgarity outright as an escape from the mock seriousness of the middle class and its sensitive chatter, treating lightheartedness as a positive social good rather than a lapse.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: The cultural counter-position to sincerity-driven media: a real and recurring demand for consequence-free silliness that periodically reprices entertainment formats.
insights.quote: I believe in frivolity. I’m all for it. I favor the vulgar.
insights.locator: In any case, I have no problem defending

insights.claim: Shakespeare wrote for an audience a third of which stood in the pit drinking ale and throwing food, and gave them Falstaff — evidence that serious art and crowd-pleasing vulgarity have never been separable.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: A durable argument against writing off mass-market low culture: the canonical products were built for exactly that audience.
insights.quote: Shakespeare knew his audience. They were inseparable from the air he breathed. He gave them Falstaff.
insights.locator: Admittedly, this is ridiculous stuff

insights.claim: Very little separates a tabloid talk-show guest from a character in serious drama — Uncle Vanya on Jenny’s stage would read as a compulsively obnoxious man in a severe midlife crisis.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Genre, not content, determines whether a life reads as tragic or ridiculous — a framing lever in every narrative-driven market.
insights.quote: Farce is just drama in clown shoes.
insights.locator: Watching Jenny Jones, I often sensed

insights.claim: The guests’ own bargain was that bringing their mess onto television made it theirs and gave them something to laugh about for years, and everyone involved knew the couple would marry anyway.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Participants in humiliation formats are often willing partners extracting durable social capital — the exploitation frame understates their agency.
insights.locator: For let’s face it, Ken and Cindi
